summary: Evolves the Interfaces group of MIB-II, describing managed objects for network interfaces so SNMP can show their state and traffic. It was replaced by RFC 2233.

plainLanguage.summary: SNMP management tables describe network interfaces. This RFC reworks the interfaces table after years of practice showed the old one was too simple: it splits an interface into its separate layers, allows interfaces to be added and removed while running, and adds 64-bit counters so that fast links do not wrap too often.

questions: what is the interfaces group mib
subtitle: How SNMP should describe a network interface, revised after years of trying to fit real interfaces into the old model.

tldr.problem: The MIB-II interfaces group described one row per interface and one media-specific MIB per interface type, but real interfaces stack several layers, appear and disappear while running, and count faster than a 32-bit counter can hold.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC reworks the interfaces group into five tables: the original ifTable, an extended ifXTable with 64-bit counters, an ifStackTable that records which sub-layer runs on top of which, and two generic tables for interface tests and receive addresses.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1573 was a Proposed Standard and it obsoleted RFC 1229. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 2233.

today: RFC 1573 was a Proposed Standard published in January 1994 and it obsoleted RFC 1229. It has since been obsoleted by RFC 2233.

sections.title: What the Interfaces Group Does
sections.content:
The memo defines a portion of the Management Information Base for use with network management protocols, and in particular describes managed objects used for managing network interfaces. It discusses the interfaces group of MIB-II, especially the experience gained from defining numerous media-specific MIB modules for use with the interfaces group to manage the various sub-layers beneath the internetwork layer. It proposes clarifications to, and extensions of, the architectural issues in the model then used for the interfaces group.

The memo also includes a MIB module. As well as adding new MIB definitions to support the architectural extensions, the module re-specifies the interfaces group of MIB-II in a manner that is both compliant to the SNMPv2 SMI and semantically identical to the existing SNMPv1-based definitions.

The SNMPv2 Network Management Framework has four major components: RFC 1442, which defines the SMI, the mechanisms used for describing and naming objects for the purpose of management; STD 17, RFC 1213, which defines MIB-II, the core set of managed objects for the Internet suite of protocols; RFC 1445, which defines the administrative and other architectural aspects of the framework; and RFC 1448, which defines the protocol used for network access to managed objects. Managed objects are accessed through a virtual information store, the Management Information Base, and each object type is named by an OBJECT IDENTIFIER, an administratively assigned name; the object type together with an object instance serves to uniquely identify a specific instantiation of the object.
sections.plainLanguage: An SNMP MIB is a list of named values a device publishes about itself. This memo is about one part of that list: the values that describe the network interfaces of the device.

sections.title: What Experience Showed Was Missing
sections.content:
One of the strengths of internetwork-layer protocols such as IP is that they are designed to run over any network interface. IP treats every protocol it runs over as a single network interface layer, and other internetwork-layer protocols take a similar view. MIB-II represents this with the interfaces group, which defines a generic set of managed objects so that any network interface can be managed in an interface-independent manner. The group also provides the means for additional managed objects specific to particular types of interface to be defined as extensions, for media-specific management. Since MIB-II was standardized, many such media-specific MIB modules have been defined.

Experience in defining them showed that the MIB-II model is too simplistic and too static for some kinds of media-specific management, and some of those modules assumed an evolution or loosening of the model. This memo proposes to document and standardize that evolution and fill in the gaps.

The specific problems the memo lists are interface numbering, interface sub-layers, virtual circuits, bit, character and fixed-length interfaces, counter size, interface speed, multicast and broadcast counters, the addition of new ifType values, and ifSpecific. On numbering, the old definition required every interface index to be smaller than the number of interfaces, which breaks when interfaces are added and removed while the device runs, a common case for a dial-up line. On sub-layers, a stack such as PPP over HDLC over an RS-232 connector has a media-specific MIB for each layer, and one row in the interfaces table cannot describe the relationship between them; the memo also notes that the current structure cannot describe upward and downward multiplexing. On counter size, a 32-bit counter wraps too soon on fast links. On speed, the ifSpeed range tops out at about 2.2 Gbit/s, which SONET's OC-48 already exceeds.
sections.plainLanguage: Every layer under IP wanted its own table, but the old model allowed only one row per interface and one table per interface type. Fast links also outran the 32-bit counters, and interfaces that come and go did not fit the numbering rule.

sections.title: The Changes: Numbers, Sub-Layers and Counters
sections.content:
For interface numbering, the memo adopts the solution of deleting the requirement that the value of ifIndex be less than ifNumber, and retaining ifNumber with its current definition. This leaves holes in the ifTable, since the index values of its rows are no longer necessarily contiguous, but SNMP's GetNext and SNMPv2's GetBulk operation easily deal with such holes. The vital constancy requirement is met by requiring that after an interface is dynamically removed, its ifIndex value is not reused by a different dynamically added interface until after the following re-initialization of the network management system. The memo recommends that ifIndex values still be assigned as relatively small integer values starting at 1, because large values would be less user-friendly, and adds a new object, ifName, holding the device's own name for the interface, since mapping interfaces to physical ports is otherwise increasingly problematic.

For sub-layers, the memo replaces the single row per interface with one conceptual row per sub-layer, each sub-layer below the internetwork layer counting as an interface, and a new ifStackTable that records the relationships between them. For example, on a router with an interface named wan1 composed of PPP running over an RS-232 port, the ifName objects for the corresponding PPP and RS-232 rows both hold the string wan1.

For counters, the memo adds 64-bit versions of the octet and packet counters, named with an ifHC prefix, because a 32-bit counter wraps too soon: on an Ethernet a stream of back-to-back full-size packets wraps ifInOctets in just over 57 minutes, on a T3 line in just over 12 minutes, on FDDI in 5.7 minutes, and on a 1-gigabit medium in as little as 34 seconds. The original combined multicast and broadcast counters are deprecated in favour of separate ones, and ifSpeed is replaced by a 64-bit gauge so that speeds above 2.2 Gbit/s can be reported.
sections.plainLanguage: The fixes are: let interface numbers be sparse but stable, give each layer of an interface its own row plus a table saying which layer sits on which, and add 64-bit counters so that a fast link does not wrap its totals every few minutes.

sections.title: The Five Tables of the New MIB
sections.content:
The MIB consists of five tables. The ifTable is the ifTable from MIB-II. The ifXTable holds objects added as a result of the interface evolution effort, or replacements for objects of the original ifTable that were deprecated because their semantics changed significantly; it also holds the objects previously in the ifExtnsTable.

The ifStackTable holds the relationships among the sub-layers of an interface, in particular which sub-layers run on top of which others. Each sub-layer corresponds to a conceptual row in the ifTable. Each row of the stack table is indexed by ifStackHigherLayer and ifStackLowerLayer, holding the ifIndex values of the two layers, and its ifStackStatus is a RowStatus, so a manager can create and remove relationships. Changing that status from active to notInService or destroy will likely have consequences up and down the interface stack, so write access is likely to be inappropriate for some types of interface.

The ifTestTable is a generic table used to perform tests on interfaces, replacing the interface test table of RFC 1229; the significant change is the replacement of the ifExtnsTestCommunity and ifExtnsTestRequestId objects by the new ifTestId, ifTestStatus and ifTestOwner objects. The ifRcvAddressTable holds the media-level addresses that the interface will receive. It too is generic, and the designers of media-specific MIBs must define exactly how it applies to their specific MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: The result is five tables: the original one, an extended one for the new counters and names, one recording how the layers stack up, one for running tests on an interface, and one for the addresses an interface listens on.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security section of the memo is one sentence: security issues are not discussed in this memo. The access control and authentication rules for reading and writing these objects belong to the SNMP framework and the SNMPv2 administrative architecture rather than to the MIB itself.
sections.plainLanguage: There is nothing about security here, because who may read or change these values is a question for the SNMP framework, not for this table.
